An order is a header row and several line rows, and they only make sense together. A transaction groups statements so that they all take effect or none of them do. JDBC connections start in auto-commit mode, where every statement is its own transaction and commits the moment it succeeds. Watch what that means. The header for order seventeen is inserted and committed. The first line is inserted and committed. The second line has a quantity of zero, violates the table's check constraint, and fails. The database now holds an order with only one of its two lines, a state no part of the program ever intended. Switch auto-commit off and the picture changes. All three inserts become one unit of work. When the second line fails, the code rolls back, and there is no trace of order seventeen at all. A fully valid order commits with both lines. Notice who does all this: the code that opens the connection decides whether to commit or roll back, exactly once, and then closes it.

Every point where your program talks to something else is a trust boundary, and the safe default is to trust nothing you have not verified. Start with TLS. Its job is not only encryption; it proves that you are talking to the server you meant to reach. Here a local HTTPS server presents a certificate it signed itself. The JDK's default trust store has never heard of it, so the handshake fails with a PKIX path building error. That failure is the protection working. The right response is to decide deliberately whom to trust: put that server's certificate into a trust store you control and configure the client with it, and the same request succeeds. The wrong response, often copied from the internet, is a trust manager that accepts every certificate, which silently removes the protection for every connection. Credentials belong in the environment or a secret store, never in source code or logs. Input from outside is bound or allow-listed. And the database account should have only the permissions its job requires.

Unit tests with fakes check your own logic. Integration tests check something different: that your code and a real protocol agree about what happens at the boundary. They do not need a shared test server or a network to do it. For the database, H2 runs in memory, so each test gets a fresh schema, real JDBC and real SQL, in milliseconds. For HTTP, the JDK's small built-in server becomes a stub: it speaks genuine HTTP, but the test decides exactly what it replies, including the awkward cases. These four tests, run by Maven, show what that buys. A saved order reads back as forty-two forty-nine. Saving the same id twice is rejected by the database's own primary key, not by code we wrote. And when the price service answers five hundred and three, the client turns it into a domain failure with a message a person can act on. Be honest about the limits too. H2 is not your production database, and a stub is not the real service. Keep a smaller suite that runs against the real things before a release.

The JVM does not load your whole program at startup. It loads, links and initialises each class lazily, the first time running code actually needs it. The class loading log makes that visible: Init is loaded to run main, main prints its first line, and only then, when the code first touches the tax table, is the nested TaxTable class loaded. Initialisation is the step that runs static initialisers, and it can fail. Here the tax rates come from configuration, one value is the text x nineteen, and parsing it throws. The first use of the class reports an ExceptionInInitializerError, carrying the real cause, the NumberFormatException. Look at the second attempt. It does not retry the initialiser. It throws NoClassDefFoundError, could not initialize class, because a class whose initialisation failed stays unusable for the life of the JVM. That message is easily confused with chapter nine's missing class. The difference is in the detail: a missing class is caused by ClassNotFoundException; could not initialize means it is there, and you must find the first error, often much earlier in the log.

The JVM does not run your bytecode the same way from start to finish. HotSpot, the usual implementation, begins by interpreting it, watching which methods run often and what types and branches they actually see. Hot methods are then compiled to native machine code in the background, while the program keeps running. The chart shows that happening. Each point is the time for one batch of two hundred thousand calls to the line-pricing method. The first batch takes about four thousand microseconds. By the tenth batch the same work takes about five hundred, eight times faster, with no change to the code. Run with dash X int, which forbids compilation, and every batch stays around seven thousand. The compilation log explains the drop: the method is compiled first by the quick C1 compiler at tier three, then by the optimising C2 compiler at tier four, after which the earlier version is retired. The percent sign marks on-stack replacement, compiling a loop while it is running. All of these details belong to HotSpot, not to the Java language.

Memory in a running Java program is split two ways. Every thread has its own stack, a pile of frames holding local variables and references, and each frame disappears when its method returns. Objects themselves live on the heap, which all threads share, and the garbage collector reclaims objects that are no longer reachable. This program builds two million orders, each a brand-new list of two line items, and each list becomes garbage one loop iteration later. The heap is capped at sixty-four mebibytes. The GC log tells the story. The collector is G1, the default on this machine. Young collections run every few milliseconds, and each one starts with around thirty-eight megabytes in use and ends with about one: almost everything was already dead. Each pause takes one to two milliseconds. That is the generational idea at work: most objects die young, so collecting the young area is cheap. When you read these logs, watch the after figure over time. If it keeps creeping up, something is holding on to objects, which is the next section.

Java's garbage collector reclaims objects that are no longer reachable. So a Java memory leak is not memory the program forgot to free; it is objects that are still reachable, through some chain of references, but are no longer useful. Here, a static map serves as a cache. Static fields are reachable for as long as the class is loaded, which is effectively forever. The cache is keyed by request id, and since every request has a new id, every request adds a ten kilobyte entry and nothing is ever removed. With a sixty-four mebibyte heap, it survives about six thousand requests and then fails with an OutOfMemoryError. Finding the culprit starts with a class histogram from jcmd. Two hundred megabytes are in byte arrays, and there are exactly twenty thousand and one Quote objects, one per request so far. When a count tracks the number of requests, something is keeping every one. The fix is to bound the cache, here a LinkedHashMap that drops its eldest entry beyond a thousand. The same workload then finishes.

When a program misbehaves in production, you usually cannot add print statements and redeploy. The JDK provides tools that observe a running JVM from the outside, and each answers a different question. JDK Flight Recorder records timed events: garbage collections, allocations, CPU samples, locks and much more. A thread dump, from jstack or jcmd, shows what every thread is doing at one moment, which is how we found the deadlock in chapter ten. Heap evidence, from a class histogram or a full heap dump, shows what is alive, which is how we found the leak. Here we recorded the garbage-producing program with the profile settings. jfr summary counts the events by type: allocation samples, seven garbage collections, a handful of execution samples. jfr print shows one collection in full, a six point four millisecond G1 pause. And the hot-methods view ranks where the CPU samples landed. Evidence has a cost. This tenth-of-a-second program took about half a second with recording on, mostly start-up. Measure the overhead in your own setting before relying on it.

Measuring performance on the JVM is harder than it looks, because the JIT compiler optimises the program you actually wrote, not the one you meant to test. Here are two loops doing the same arithmetic two hundred million times. In the first, the result of each call is thrown away. In the second, the results are summed and the sum is stored. The first loop takes three milliseconds, then one, then zero. That is not fast arithmetic; that is no arithmetic. The compiler proved that nothing used the results and removed the work entirely. The second loop, whose result is used, takes about half a second, which is the real cost. There are other traps too. Timing the first few iterations measures the interpreter, as the warm-up chart showed. A single run on a single machine is weak evidence. And constant inputs invite constant folding. So follow a method: start from a measured symptom, form one hypothesis, make one change, and re-measure under the same conditions. For microbenchmarks, use a harness such as JMH, which exists to defeat exactly these traps.

An application is never finished, because the ground under it keeps moving. New JDK releases deprecate and eventually remove APIs, libraries publish updates, and security fixes arrive that you must apply quickly. The cheapest time to discover a problem is before the upgrade, and the JDK can help. Compiling this small legacy class, javac warns that sun dot misc dot Unsafe is an internal proprietary API that may be removed. jdeprscan, asked for APIs deprecated for removal, flags Runtime dot runFinalization. And jdeps lists every dependency on JDK internals, naming the module they come from. Treat these tools as detectors rather than guarantees: here jdeprscan reported only one of the deprecated calls in the file. Staying current is a habit. Run on a supported JDK and apply its updates, and move dependencies forward in small, tested steps rather than giant leaps. Then release in stages: pin and record every version, scan for known vulnerabilities, roll out to a small canary first, watch the evidence, and keep a rollback that you have actually tested.

This course began with a single line of output: three items at twelve fifty plus shipping, forty-two forty-nine. The same order program now has a shape worth reviewing as a whole. Work through it as a lifecycle. Data comes in across boundaries: a CSV import with an explicit charset and validation, a price service called with timeouts and safe retries, and configuration loaded from the classpath and overridden at launch. It lands in a domain core that does no I/O at all: objects that guard their invariants, interfaces for the parts that vary, and collections and streams for the arithmetic. It leaves through more boundaries: database transactions, files replaced atomically, and work spread across bounded, cancellable threads. Around all of it sits evidence: unit and integration tests, a pinned and repeatable build, and runtime diagnostics. For any change you make from here, ask three questions. Which contract does it touch? What happens if it fails half-way? And what evidence will show it works? From here, specialise: frameworks, algorithms, distributed systems, performance or security. Practical expertise grows with experience.
